# Audio Signal Processing Apparatus with Depth-Adaptive Rendering

## Overview

The present disclosure relates to an audio signal processing apparatus configured to process audio signals in conjunction with three-dimensional visual content, ensuring that the perceived spatial position of audio sources is dynamically adapted to the depth-rendering characteristics of the display device on which the corresponding three-dimensional images are presented. The apparatus comprises several interconnected functional components, each contributing to accurate and perceptually consistent audio-visual depth alignment.

## Receiver Component

At the core of the apparatus is a receiver (101), which is responsible for capturing an incoming audio signal. This audio signal contains audio data corresponding to at least one audio object that is associated with, or linked to, a three-dimensional image being displayed to the user. In other words, rather than treating audio as an independent stream unrelated to the visual content, the received signal is structured such that individual audio objects—discrete sound sources within the overall audio mix—correspond directly to visual elements or objects present in the accompanying three-dimensional imagery.

In addition to the audio data itself, the received audio signal incorporates supplementary depth position data. This data specifies a target depth position for the first audio object, effectively indicating where, in three-dimensional space, the audio source is intended to be perceived relative to the viewer. This target depth position is typically derived from the original production or authoring of the content, reflecting the intended spatial relationship between the audio object and its corresponding visual counterpart within the three-dimensional scene.

## Determiner Component

Because different three-dimensional display technologies exhibit varying capabilities in rendering depth—some displays may only accurately represent a limited range of perceived depth, while others may support a wider or narrower range—the apparatus includes a determiner (107). The determiner is tasked with establishing the visual rendering depth range that is appropriate for, and specific to, the target three-dimensional display being used to present the three-dimensional image to the viewer.

This visual rendering depth range represents the boundaries within which the display can accurately and comfortably render depth cues, taking into account factors such as screen size, viewing distance, display technology (e.g., stereoscopic, autostereoscopic, or other three-dimensional display methods), and any inherent limitations that may affect the perceived depth fidelity. By determining this range dynamically or in accordance with the specific display in use, the apparatus ensures that subsequent audio processing is tailored to the actual visual depth capabilities of the presentation system, rather than relying on a fixed or assumed depth range that may not correspond to the real-world rendering conditions.

## Mapper Component

Building upon the depth position data received for the audio object and the visual rendering depth range established by the determiner, the apparatus further includes a mapper (109). The primary function of the mapper is to convert the target depth position—originally specified in the audio signal—into a corresponding rendering depth position for the audio object. This mapping process is not performed in isolation; rather, it is explicitly dependent on, and informed by, the visual rendering depth range determined for the target three-dimensional display.

Through this dependency, the mapper effectively translates the intended depth position of the audio object into a depth position that is realistically achievable and consistent with what the viewer will perceive visually on the specific display being used. This ensures that the audio rendering depth remains coherent with the visual rendering depth, even when the display's depth capabilities differ from the original authoring assumptions.

## Alignment of Audio and Visual Depth Positions

A particularly important function of the mapper (109) is its ability to adjust the sound source positions of audio objects so that they align closely with the depth positions of their corresponding visual objects within the three-dimensional image. This alignment is especially critical within the portion of the depth range where the display is capable of accurately and reliably rendering depth information.

By prioritizing accurate alignment within this reliable rendering range, the mapper helps maintain a consistent and immersive audio-visual experience for the viewer. Should the target depth position fall outside the range that the display can accurately render, the mapper may apply appropriate scaling, compression, or other adaptive techniques to map the audio object's depth position into the nearest perceptually appropriate position within the supported range, thereby minimizing any perceptual mismatch between what is seen and what is heard.

## Summary

In summary, the audio signal processing apparatus described herein provides an integrated solution for dynamically aligning audio object depth positions with the depth-rendering capabilities of a target three-dimensional display. Through the coordinated operation of the receiver (101), determiner (107), and mapper (109), the apparatus captures audio data and associated depth position information, establishes the relevant visual rendering depth range for the display in use, and maps the audio object's target depth position into a rendering depth position optimized for accurate perceptual alignment with the corresponding visual content. This approach enhances the overall coherence and realism of three-dimensional audio-visual presentations across a variety of display technologies and configurations.

# Audio Signal Processing Apparatus for Depth-Synchronized Audio-Visual Rendering

## Background and Technical Field

In modern three-dimensional (3D) display systems, visual content is rendered with depth information that creates the perception of objects existing at varying distances from the viewer. However, a persistent challenge in multimedia systems has been ensuring that the audio component of such content—particularly positional audio associated with specific on-screen objects—accurately reflects the same depth characteristics as the visual elements. When audio objects and their corresponding visual counterparts fail to align in perceived depth, the overall immersive experience is degraded, and the sense of realism intended by 3D content creators is undermined. This apparatus addresses that gap by providing a systematic method for adapting audio depth positioning to match the rendering capabilities and characteristics of the specific display being used.

## Overview of the Apparatus

The audio signal processing apparatus described herein comprises several interoperating components designed to receive, analyze, and transform audio positional data so that it corresponds precisely with the depth rendering capabilities of a target display device. The apparatus is particularly suited for use in home theater systems, cinema environments, augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) platforms, and any multimedia system in which audio objects must be spatially synchronized with 3D visual content.

## Reception of Audio Data with Target Depth Position Information

At the core of the apparatus is a receiving unit configured to accept incoming audio data that includes embedded or associated target depth position information. This depth position information indicates the intended perceptual depth—that is, how far in front of or behind the display plane a particular sound source (audio object) should appear to originate—based on the depth position of its corresponding visual object in the original 3D content. Such information may be encoded as metadata accompanying the audio stream, derived from content authoring tools, or extracted from an associated video signal.

The receiving unit is capable of parsing multi-channel or object-based audio formats, identifying discrete audio objects, and extracting their respective target depth values, typically expressed as a position along a depth axis (e.g., near-to-far or a defined numerical range) relative to a reference display plane.

## Determination of Target Display Depth Rendering Range

Because different 3D display devices—including autostereoscopic displays, active/passive stereoscopic displays, holographic displays, or multi-view displays—possess distinct capabilities regarding how much positive or negative depth they can accurately render, the apparatus includes a depth range determination unit. This unit assesses or retrieves information about the target display’s maximum and minimum renderable depth boundaries, sometimes referred to as its "depth budget" or "comfortable viewing volume."

This determination may be accomplished through several approaches: querying a lookup table containing display specifications, receiving calibration data transmitted directly from the display device, or dynamically calculating the depth range based on viewing distance, screen size, and other environmental parameters relevant to visual comfort and perceptual accuracy.

## Mapping of Target Depth Position to Rendering Depth Position

Once both the target depth position of the audio object and the determined depth rendering range of the display are known, a mapping unit (or "mapper") performs the critical function of translating the original target depth position into an appropriate rendering depth position suitable for the specific display in use. This mapping process ensures that even if the target display's depth rendering range differs from the range assumed during original content creation, the relative depth relationships among audio objects are preserved as faithfully as possible.

The mapper may employ linear scaling, non-linear compression, or other transformation algorithms to fit the original depth values within the constraints of the target display's range. For instance, if original content was designed for a display capable of extreme depth extension but is being rendered on a display with a more limited depth range, the mapper compresses the audio object's target depth position proportionally, maintaining relative ordering and perceptual consistency without exceeding the display's rendering limits.

## Synchronization of Audio Sound Sources and Visual Objects

The ultimate output of this mapping process is a set of rendering depth positions for each audio sound source that accurately corresponds to the depth positions of their associated visual objects as they appear on the specific 3D display. By ensuring this correspondence, the apparatus enables audio reproduction systems—such as multi-speaker arrays, soundbars with virtual surround processing, or headphone-based binaural rendering systems—to generate sound that appears to emanate from the same spatial depth as the visual object a listener is observing.

## Advantages and Applications

By dynamically adjusting audio depth positioning according to the specific characteristics of the target display, this apparatus provides several advantages: it enhances the perceptual realism and immersion of 3D audiovisual content, ensures cross-platform compatibility of depth-encoded audio regardless of variations in display hardware, and reduces potential audio-visual depth mismatch that could otherwise cause perceptual confusion or discomfort for viewers. This makes the apparatus valuable for applications ranging from cinematic post-production and broadcast systems to consumer electronics, gaming platforms, and immersive AR/VR experiences where precise depth-based audio-visual alignment is essential to user experience.

# Patent Abstract

**AUDIO SIGNAL PROCESSING APPARATUS AND METHOD FOR DEPTH-ADAPTIVE AUDIO OBJECT RENDERING IN THREE-DIMENSIONAL DISPLAY SYSTEMS**

An audio signal processing apparatus and method are disclosed for dynamically adjusting the perceived depth positioning of audio objects to correspond with the visual rendering depth range of a three-dimensional (3D) display device. The apparatus includes a depth range acquisition unit configured to obtain display-specific depth parameters, including maximum and minimum perceivable depth values associated with a target 3D display, which may vary according to screen size, viewing distance, or display technology. An audio object depth extraction unit analyzes metadata associated with one or more audio objects within an input audio signal to determine an original or intended depth position for each object, said depth position corresponding to a source-side visual depth range associated with content authored for a reference display configuration. A depth mapping unit is configured to compute a scaling and/or offset transformation that maps the original audio object depth values from the source depth range to the target display's depth range, thereby generating adjusted depth position values that preserve relative depth relationships among multiple audio objects while conforming to the physical or perceptual depth constraints of the target display. A rendering unit applies the adjusted depth position values to corresponding audio rendering parameters, including interaural time difference, interaural level difference, direct-to-reverberant energy ratio, and/or binaural or multichannel gain coefficients, to synthesize output audio signals in which the perceived auditory depth of each object is spatially aligned with its corresponding visual depth as rendered on the 3D display. The apparatus may further include a synchronization unit that receives display depth range information via a metadata interface or display identification signal, enabling automatic, content-adaptive audio-visual depth matching without requiring manual calibration. The disclosed apparatus improves audio-visual perceptual consistency, reduces sensory conflict between visual and auditory depth cues, and enhances immersive experience across heterogeneous 3D display environments having differing depth rendering capabilities.

# Technical Disclosure: System for Aligning Audio Object Depth with 3D Display Capabilities

## Field of the Disclosure

This disclosure relates to audio-visual synchronization systems, and more particularly to systems and methods for dynamically aligning perceived audio object depth with the depth range capabilities of a three-dimensional (3D) display device to ensure perceptual consistency between visual and auditory spatial cues.

## Background

Modern immersive audio formats (e.g., object-based audio) encode positional metadata for individual audio elements, including depth (Z-axis) positioning relative to a nominal screen plane. Concurrently, 3D display systems—including stereoscopic displays, autostereoscopic displays, light-field displays, and volumetric displays—render visual content with varying depth budgets depending on panel size, viewing distance, disparity limits, and comfort constraints.

A mismatch arises when audio object depth metadata specifies a depth position that exceeds or otherwise does not correspond to the depth range that a target display is capable of rendering. For example, audio metadata may indicate an object should be perceived 2 meters in front of the screen plane, while the display's maximum comfortable disparity only supports 0.5 meters of forward depth. This mismatch causes a perceptual disconnect: a listener/viewer hears an object emerging strongly toward them while seeing it rendered near the screen plane, breaking immersion and potentially causing sensory conflict or discomfort.

Existing systems typically process audio depth and visual depth independently, with no mechanism for reconciling the two based on actual display capability. There is a need for a system that receives audio object depth metadata, determines the depth rendering capability of a target 3D display, and maps the audio depth into the display's achievable range in a manner that preserves relative spatial relationships and perceptual intent.

## Summary

The disclosed system comprises three primary functional components:

1. **A Receiver Component** configured to obtain audio object depth metadata and 3D display depth capability information.
2. **A Determiner Component** configured to establish the depth rendering range/capability of the target display and to evaluate the input audio depth values against that range.
3. **A Mapper Component** configured to transform (remap) the audio object depth values into an adjusted depth value set that is compatible with the determined display capability, while preserving relative depth ordering and perceptual proportionality among audio objects.

The system may be implemented in a set-top box, AV receiver, television SoC, mobile device, gaming console, or as a software module within a media playback pipeline.

---

## Detailed Description

### 1. System Overview

```
   ┌─────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
   │                 │     │                  │     │                 │
   │    RECEIVER     │────▶│    DETERMINER    │────▶│     MAPPER      │
   │   COMPONENT     │     │    COMPONENT     │     │    COMPONENT    │
   │                 │     │                  │     │                 │
   └─────────────────┘     └──────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘
          │                         │                        │
          ▼                         ▼                        ▼
   Audio object depth      Display depth range        Adjusted audio
   metadata + display      + depth conflict           depth metadata
   capability signaling    analysis                   → renderer
```

### 2. Receiver Component

The Receiver Component is configured to obtain, from one or more sources, the following inputs:

**a) Audio Object Depth Metadata**
- Per-object Z-axis position (depth), typically expressed relative to a nominal screen/reference plane (e.g., in meters, normalized units [-1, 1], or perceived-distance categories).
- Optionally, per-object depth trajectories (time-varying depth over the duration of the content).
- Optionally, depth confidence/priority weighting (e.g., dialogue objects may be flagged as depth-critical, while ambient effects may be flagged as depth-flexible).
- Metadata may be extracted from bitstream side-channel data (e.g., object audio metadata in immersive formats), from an accompanying manifest, or inferred from scene descriptors.

**b) 3D Display Depth Capability Signaling**
- Display type (stereoscopic, autostereoscopic, light-field, volumetric, 2D-with-simulated-depth, etc.)
- Maximum negative parallax (behind-screen depth budget)
- Maximum positive parallax (in-front-of-screen / audience-side depth budget)
- Viewing distance assumptions or actual measured viewing distance (e.g., via companion device or camera-based sensing)
- Panel size and pixel pitch (used to convert disparity limits to physical/perceptual depth units)
- Dynamic capability updates, e.g., a display operating in a reduced-depth "comfort mode" or a mode change (2D↔3D)

This capability information may be received via EDID/HDMI extensions, a display-side API, manufacturer configuration profile, or real-time telemetry from the display device.

The Receiver Component outputs a normalized representation of both audio depth data and display capability data to the Determiner Component, using a common depth unit convention (e.g., normalized depth units relative to screen plane, with defined positive/negative sign convention).

### 3. Determiner Component

The Determiner Component performs the following operations:

**a) Depth Capability Resolution**
Given the raw display capability inputs, the Determiner computes an effective renderable depth range: `[D_min, D_max]`, where `D_min` denotes the maximum supported behind-screen depth and `D_max` denotes the maximum supported in-front-of-screen depth. This may involve:
- Converting disparity limits (in pixels or arcminutes) into distance units, accounting for viewing distance and panel geometry.
- Applying viewer-comfort derating factors (e.g., limiting usable range to 80% of the theoretical maximum to avoid vergence-accommodation conflict).
- Adjusting for any dynamic display mode currently active.

**b) Audio Depth Range Analysis**
The Determiner analyzes the received audio object depth metadata to establish the depth range spanned by the content: `[A_min, A_max]`, across all objects and, optionally, over time (for time-varying depth trajectories).

**c) Conflict/Mismatch Determination**
The Determiner compares `[A_min, A_max]` against `[D_min, D_max]` to determine whether one or more audio objects specify depth values outside the display's renderable range. It computes:
- A per-object overflow/underflow metric.
- An aggregate mismatch severity score.
- A classification of mismatch type (e.g., "exceeds forward depth only," "exceeds both directions," "within tolerance").

**d) Mapping Strategy Selection**
Based on the mismatch classification, the Determiner selects an appropriate mapping strategy to be applied by the Mapper Component, such as:
- **Linear rescaling**: proportionally compress the entire audio depth range into the display range.
- **Soft clipping / knee compression**: preserve near-screen depth fidelity and only compress objects near the extremes.
- **Priority-weighted mapping**: preserve depth-critical objects (e.g., dialogue) with minimal adjustment while more aggressively compressing lower-priority objects.
- **Piecewise mapping**: apply different scaling factors in different depth bands.

The Determiner outputs the resolved display depth range, the mismatch analysis, and the selected mapping strategy/parameters to the Mapper Component.

### 4. Mapper Component

The Mapper Component receives the original audio object depth metadata, the target display range `[D_min, D_max]`, and the selected mapping strategy, and produces adjusted depth metadata for each audio object.

**Example mapping functions:**

*Linear rescaling:*
```
A'(t) = D_min + (A(t) - A_min) × (D_max - D_min) / (A_max - A_min)
```

*Priority-weighted piecewise mapping:*
```
For each object i with priority weight w_i:
  scale_i = f(w_i, mismatch_severity)
  A'_i(t) = clamp(A_i(t) × scale_i, D_min, D_max)
```

*Soft-knee compression near boundaries:*
```
A'(t) = A(t)                         if |A(t)| < knee_threshold
A'(t) = sign(A(t)) × soft_curve(...)  if |A(t)| ≥ knee_threshold
```

The Mapper additionally ensures:
- **Relative ordering preservation**: if object X was perceptually closer than object Y in the original mix, this relationship is preserved post-mapping (unless explicitly overridden by priority weighting).
- **Temporal smoothness**: depth trajectories are remapped without introducing discontinuities or artifacts (e.g., using smoothing/interpolation across frame boundaries).
- **Synchronization**: adjusted depth metadata is timestamp-aligned with the corresponding audio frames/objects and, where applicable, with the corresponding visual depth cues in the video pipeline, so that the rendering engine (audio spatializer / binaural renderer / speaker panning engine) applies depth cues consistent with the display's visual depth rendering.

The Mapper outputs the adjusted audio object depth metadata to the downstream audio rendering pipeline (e.g., object-based renderer, binaural/HRTF processor, or channel-based downmixer with depth-dependent gain/EQ/reverb cues).

### 5. Optional Feedback and Dynamic Adaptation

In one embodiment, the system operates continuously during playback:
- The Receiver monitors for display capability changes (e.g., user switching 3D modes, changing viewing distance detected by a sensor).
- The Determiner re-evaluates the mismatch and mapping strategy in response to such changes.
- The Mapper applies updated mappings in real time, with cross-fading/smoothing to avoid perceptible jumps in audio depth.

### 6. Example Use Case

A movie encoded with immersive object-based audio specifies a helicopter sound object with depth metadata placing it 3 meters in front of the screen during a flyover scene. The target display is an autostereoscopic panel with a comfort-limited maximum forward depth of 0.6 meters.

- **Receiver** obtains the helicopter object's depth trajectory (0m → 3m → 0m) and the display's capability profile (`D_max = 0.6m`, `D_min = -1.2m`).
- **Determiner** identifies that the trajectory exceeds `D_max` by up to 2.4m, classifies this as "forward-depth overflow," and selects a soft-knee compression strategy to preserve the sense of motion while respecting comfort limits.
- **Mapper** remaps the trajectory to (0m → 0.6m → 0m) using the soft-knee function, preserving temporal shape and directional motion cues while keeping perceived depth within the display's renderable/comfortable range, and outputs synchronized adjusted metadata to the spatial audio renderer.

The result is that the auditory sense of the helicopter's approach remains proportionally consistent with what the display can visually render, avoiding audio-visual depth conflict.

---

## Alternative Embodiments

- The Determiner may incorporate machine-learning-based mismatch classification trained on perceptual studies correlating audio-visual depth conflict with viewer discomfort reports.
- The system may be extended to multi-display or multi-viewer environments (e.g., glasses-free multi-view displays), where the Determiner computes a depth range applicable across all supported viewing zones.
- The Mapper may additionally adjust related audio rendering parameters (e.g., loudness, early reflections, Doppler-derived pitch cues) in coordination with depth remapping to reinforce the perceptually consistent depth impression.
- The system may be applied in reverse: given fixed audio depth metadata, the system could recommend or automatically configure a compatible 3D display depth setting.

## Advantages

- Reduces audio-visual perceptual conflict in 3D media playback.
- Preserves creative intent (relative depth relationships, motion traject

# INVENTION SUMMARY

## Title
**System and Method for Synchronizing Spatial Audio Depth Cues with Stereoscopic 3D Video Rendering Constraints**

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to multimedia rendering systems, and more particularly to systems and methods for dynamically coordinating perceived audio depth positioning with the depth rendering capabilities and limitations of stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) display systems, so as to maintain perceptual coherence between audiovisual depth cues presented to a viewer/listener.

## Background

Stereoscopic 3D video systems render depth through binocular disparity between left-eye and right-eye image pairs. Such systems are subject to finite depth budgets, commonly bounded by a comfortable disparity range (positive parallax for background objects and negative parallax for foreground/theater-space objects), beyond which visual artifacts such as diplopia, ghosting, vergence-accommodation conflict, or viewer discomfort may occur. Content is therefore often depth-graded, clipped, or dynamically remapped to remain within a display-safe or comfort-safe disparity envelope.

Concurrently, spatial audio systems (e.g., object-based audio, ambisonics, binaural rendering, or multi-channel panning systems) are capable of positioning virtual sound sources at arbitrary perceived depths relative to the listener, using cues including interaural time/level differences, direct-to-reverberant energy ratios, spectral filtering, distance-dependent loudness attenuation, and motion parallax cues.

A problem arises when spatial audio depth cues indicate a sound source position (e.g., strongly negative parallax, "in front of the screen") that exceeds, contradicts, or is inconsistent with the depth position at which the corresponding visual object is *actually* rendered after the video pipeline applies disparity clipping, dynamic depth remapping, or comfort-based rescaling. This audio-visual depth mismatch can degrade perceptual immersion, break cross-modal object correspondence, and, in some cases, exacerbate visual discomfort by reinforcing a depth cue that the visual system has been forced to suppress or compress.

Existing audio rendering pipelines and video depth-management pipelines are generally implemented as independent subsystems with no mechanism for exchanging depth-constraint metadata, and no method exists for a spatial audio renderer to become aware of, and adapt to, the *actual* depth budget being applied downstream in the video pipeline at render time.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses the foregoing limitations by providing a system and method for dynamically synchronizing spatial audio depth cue generation with the operative depth-rendering constraints of a stereoscopic 3D video pipeline, such that perceived audio object depth remains perceptually consistent with the depth at which corresponding visual content is actually displayed.

In one aspect, the invention comprises:

1. **A depth constraint acquisition module**, configured to obtain, from a stereoscopic video rendering pipeline, one or more depth-constraint parameters including, without limitation: maximum positive parallax, maximum negative parallax, a dynamically computed comfort-safe disparity range, per-frame or per-scene depth remapping curves, and/or clipping thresholds currently being applied to source depth/disparity data.

2. **An audio depth mapping module**, configured to receive intended or authored spatial audio object depth values (e.g., from object-based audio metadata, positional audio engine coordinates, or game/VR engine scene graphs) and to remap said audio depth values, in real time or near-real time, into an adjusted audio depth value that conforms to the depth-constraint parameters obtained from the video pipeline.

3. **A cross-modal correspondence engine**, configured to associate individual spatial audio objects with corresponding visual objects or screen regions (via object identifiers, scene graph correspondence, spatial coordinate matching, or metadata tagging), such that audio depth remapping may be applied selectively, on a per-object basis, rather than uniformly across an entire audio scene.

4. **A synchronized rendering output stage**, configured to render the remapped spatial audio depth cues (via binaural processing, panning coefficient adjustment, distance-cue attenuation, reverberation adjustment, or multi-channel object rendering) in temporal and perceptual synchrony with the corresponding stereoscopic video frames, such that the combined audiovisual presentation maintains cross-modal depth coherence within the constraints of the display's rendering envelope.

In certain embodiments, the depth-constraint parameters are computed dynamically per-scene or per-frame (e.g., where a video rendering pipeline applies content-adaptive disparity remapping), and the audio depth mapping module is configured to update its remapping function accordingly on a corresponding frame-synchronous or scene-synchronous basis, using a shared timing/synchronization signal or metadata channel between the video and audio subsystems.

In further embodiments, the audio depth mapping module applies a non-linear or perceptually-weighted compression function (analogous to tone-mapping in high-dynamic-range video) to preserve relative depth ordering and relative depth salience among multiple audio objects, even where the absolute depth range must be compressed to fit within the video-derived constraint envelope.

In additional embodiments, the system further comprises a user-adjustable depth-coherence preference setting, permitting the degree of audio-visual depth synchronization (e.g., full conformance, partial conformance, or independent rendering) to be configured according to user comfort or content-creator intent, and a discomfort-mitigation mode wherein detected extreme visual depth clipping events (e.g., due to viewer proximity detection or display-type constraints) trigger a corresponding attenuation of audio depth cue intensity to reduce cross-modal sensory conflict.

## Advantages

The disclosed system provides, among other benefits: (i) improved perceptual coherence between audio and visual depth cues in stereoscopic 3D content; (ii) reduced viewer discomfort associated with vergence-accommodation conflict reinforced by contradictory audio depth cues; (iii) a metadata-driven architecture enabling interoperability across heterogeneous video rendering pipelines and audio rendering engines; and (iv) applicability to pre-rendered content, real-time gaming/VR/AR environments, and adaptive streaming contexts alike.

---

# APPARATUS AND METHOD FOR REMAPPING DEPTH POSITION METADATA FOR AUDIO OBJECTS BASED ON DISPLAY-ACHIEVABLE DEPTH RANGE

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to audio-visual signal processing, and more particularly to apparatus and methods for receiving, interpreting, and remapping depth position metadata associated with audio objects in accordance with a depth range achievable by a display device.

## BACKGROUND

In audio-visual presentation systems configured to render three-dimensional or depth-enhanced content, audio objects are often associated with metadata specifying a perceived spatial position, including a depth component indicating a distance of the audio object relative to a reference plane, such as a screen plane. However, display devices employed to render corresponding visual content may exhibit varying capabilities with respect to achievable depth range, owing to differences in screen size, viewing distance, stereoscopic disparity limits, or other display-specific characteristics. Accordingly, a need exists for apparatus and methods capable of adaptively remapping received depth position metadata to conform to the depth range achievable by a particular display, so as to maintain perceptual consistency between audio and visual depth cues.

## SUMMARY

In accordance with at least one embodiment, there is provided an apparatus comprising a receiving unit configured to receive an audio object and associated metadata, the metadata including at least one depth position value indicative of an intended depth position of the audio object relative to a reference plane; a display characteristic acquisition unit configured to obtain, determine, or otherwise acquire display depth range information indicative of a depth range achievable by a display device; and a remapping unit configured to generate a remapped depth position value by transforming the at least one depth position value based at least in part on the acquired display depth range information, and to output the remapped depth position value in association with the audio object for use in subsequent audio rendering.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### 1. General Configuration

Referring now to the drawings, in which like reference numerals designate like or corresponding parts throughout the several views, there is shown in **FIG. 1** a block diagram illustrating an apparatus 100 according to at least one embodiment of the present disclosure.

The apparatus 100 comprises a metadata receiving unit 110, a display depth range acquisition unit 120, a depth position remapping unit 130, and an output unit 140, each of which may be implemented by one or more processors, controllers, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), or any suitable combination of hardware, firmware, and/or software instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by processing circuitry.

### 2. Metadata Receiving Unit

The metadata receiving unit 110 is configured to receive, via an input interface, an audio bitstream, audio object stream, or associated data structure comprising one or more audio objects and corresponding metadata. In at least one embodiment, the metadata includes, for each audio object, a depth position value, which may be expressed as a scalar quantity, a normalized coordinate, a signed offset relative to a screen plane, or any other suitable representation indicative of an intended perceptual depth of the audio object. The depth position value may further be associated with a temporal indicator, such that the depth position of a given audio object may vary over the duration of the associated audio-visual content.

In some embodiments, the metadata may further comprise a reference depth range associated with a reference or authoring display, such that the received depth position value is expressed relative to a known or assumed depth range at the time of content creation. This reference depth range may be explicitly signaled within the metadata, or may be inferred based on default parameters associated with a content format or standard.

### 3. Display Depth Range Acquisition Unit

The display depth range acquisition unit 120 is configured to obtain display depth range information indicative of a maximum achievable depth range of a display device intended to present visual content associated with the audio object. In at least one embodiment, the display depth range information may be obtained by querying the display device directly, for example, via a communication interface such as HDMI, DisplayPort, or a network-based control protocol. In other embodiments, the display depth range information may be retrieved from a locally or remotely stored profile associated with a display identifier, may be received as a user-configurable parameter, or may be derived based on one or more sensed characteristics, including but not limited to screen size, resolution, viewing distance, and stereoscopic baseline.

It will be appreciated that the display depth range information may be expressed in a variety of formats, including, without limitation, a minimum and maximum depth value, a signed range relative to a screen plane, a set of discrete depth planes, or a continuous depth function.

### 4. Depth Position Remapping Unit

The depth position remapping unit 130 is configured to receive the depth position value from the metadata receiving unit 110 and the display depth range information from the display depth range acquisition unit 120, and to generate, based thereon, a remapped depth position value.

In at least one embodiment, the remapping unit 130 is configured to apply a scaling function to the received depth position value, such that the remapped depth position value falls within the achievable depth range of the display device while preserving, to the extent possible, the relative depth ordering and perceptual spacing among a plurality of audio objects. The scaling function may comprise a linear mapping, a piecewise-linear mapping, a non-linear compression function such as a logarithmic or sigmoidal function, or a perceptually-weighted mapping derived empirically or through psychoacoustic modeling.

In another embodiment, the remapping unit 130 is configured to apply a clipping or clamping operation, wherein depth position values exceeding the achievable depth range are constrained to a nearest boundary value of said range, while depth position values within the achievable range remain substantially unmodified.

In yet another embodiment, the remapping unit 130 may be configured to apply a dynamic remapping function that varies over time based on one or more of: a scene change indicator, a plurality of concurrently active audio objects, an overall depth budget associated with the display, or a user-defined preference indicating a desired depth intensity.

The remapping unit 130 may further be configured to generate the remapped depth position value based on a ratio between the achievable depth range of the display device and a reference depth range associated with the received metadata, such that:

**D_remapped = f(D_received, R_display, R_reference)**

wherein D_received represents the received depth position value, R_display represents the achievable depth range of the display device, R_reference represents the reference depth range associated with the metadata, and f represents a predetermined or adaptively determined mapping function.

### 5. Output Unit

The output unit 140 is configured to output the remapped depth position value in association with the corresponding audio object, for example, by generating updated metadata incorporating the remapped depth position value, or by providing the remapped depth position value to a downstream audio rendering unit configured to spatially render the audio object in accordance with the remapped depth position value.

### 6. Alternative Embodiments

In at least one alternative embodiment, the apparatus 100 further comprises a synchronization unit configured to align the remapped depth position value with a corresponding visual depth cue associated with a visual object displayed on the display device, so as to maintain audio-visual depth congruence.

In another alternative embodiment, the remapping unit 130 is configured to generate the remapped depth position value further based on a plurality of display depth ranges corresponding to a plurality of display devices, such as in a multi-display or distributed rendering environment, wherein the remapped depth position value is generated so as to be compatible with each of the plurality of display devices, or wherein a plurality of remapped depth position values are generated, each corresponding to a respective display device of the plurality of display devices.

It is understood that the various units described herein need not be physically distinct components, and that the functions attributed to each unit may be performed by a single processor executing appropriate instructions, or distributed among a plurality of processors, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

## CLAIMS (Exemplary)

**1.** An apparatus comprising:
a receiving unit configured to receive an audio object and associated metadata, the metadata comprising a depth position value indicative of an intended depth position of the audio object relative to a reference plane;
an acquisition unit configured to acquire display depth range information indicative of a depth range achievable by a display device; and
a remapping unit configured to generate a remapped depth position value by transforming the depth position value based on the display depth range information, and to output the remapped depth position value in association with the audio object.

**2.** The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the remapping unit is configured to apply a scaling function such that the remapped depth position value is constrained within the depth range achievable by the display device.

**3.** The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the metadata further comprises a reference depth range, and wherein the remapping unit generates the remapped depth position value based on a ratio between the display depth range information and the reference depth range.

**4.** The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the remapping unit is configured to apply a clamping operation such that depth position values exceeding the display depth range information are constrained to a boundary value thereof.

**5.** The apparatus of claim 1, further comprising a synchronization unit configured to align the remapped depth position value with a visual depth cue associated with a visual object displayed on the display device.

**6.** The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the display depth range information is obtained via a communication interface configured to query the display device.

**7.** A method comprising:
receiving an audio object and associated metadata comprising a depth position value;
acquiring display depth range information indicative of a depth range achievable by a display device;
generating a remapped depth position value by transforming the depth position value based on the display depth range information; and
outputting the remapped depth position value in association with the audio object for rendering.

# Abstract

**System and Method for Correcting Depth Perception Mismatches in Audio-Visual 3D Content Playback**

Disclosed herein is a hardware apparatus (100) for detecting and correcting perceptual mismatches between audio and visual depth cues during playback of three-dimensional (3D) multimedia content. The system comprises a content input interface (102) configured to receive a multiplexed audio-visual data stream containing stereoscopic image data (104) and multi-channel audio data (106).

A depth analysis module (110) is coupled to the content input interface (102) and includes a visual depth estimation unit (112) configured to extract depth map information from the stereoscopic image data (104) using disparity calculations between left-eye and right-eye image frames. The depth analysis module (110) further comprises an audio depth estimation unit (114) configured to determine perceived audio source distance based on interaural time difference, interaural level difference, and reverberation characteristics present within the multi-channel audio data (106).

A comparator circuit (120) is operatively connected to the visual depth estimation unit (112) and the audio depth estimation unit (114), and is configured to calculate a depth discrepancy value (122) representing a difference between visually-perceived depth and audibly-perceived depth for corresponding content segments.

A correction processor (130) is responsive to the depth discrepancy value (122) and includes an audio adjustment subunit (132) configured to modify at least one audio parameter—selected from a group consisting of delay, amplitude, and spectral filtering—to shift the perceived audio depth toward alignment with the visual depth. Alternatively, or in combination, a visual adjustment subunit (134) is configured to modify stereoscopic disparity parameters within the image data (104) to shift the perceived visual depth toward alignment with the audio depth.

An output interface (140) is configured to transmit corrected audio-visual data to a display device (150) and an audio rendering device (152), thereby producing a synchronized multisensory depth experience with reduced perceptual conflict for a viewer/listener (160).

This configuration enables real-time or near-real-time correction of depth mismatches arising from encoding artifacts, transmission errors, or source content inconsistencies, thereby improving user comfort and reducing symptoms associated with sensory conflict during 3D content consumption.
